What To Expect: The clinician identifies the cause and chooses a conservative plan. Procedures, if used, are generally staged to limit irritation and pigment rebound.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually a longer-term course; procedural frequency depends on treatment and response.
Downtime & Recovery: Varies from none to several days of redness or peeling.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Aggressive treatment can worsen pigment, especially in darker skin. Treating the underlying trigger is important.
FAQs:
Q: Can body pigmentation be treated like facial pigmentation?
A: Not always. Body skin, causes and friction patterns differ, so the treatment plan should be site-specific.

Short Description: Procedural treatment aimed at making stretch marks less noticeable through collagen remodeling and pigment/texture improvement.
Full Description: Stretch marks (striae) are a type of dermal scar associated with skin stretching. They can fade naturally over time but usually cannot be completely erased. Treatment may include microneedling, fractional laser, radiofrequency or selected topical therapy depending on whether marks are newer and red or older and pale.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Early red/purple stretch marks
2. Older white stretch marks
3. Texture irregularity from striae
Key Benefits:
• Can reduce visibility of stretch marks
• May improve texture and colour contrast
• Multiple modalities can be considered
What To Expect: The clinician assesses the age and colour of the stretch marks and chooses a resurfacing or collagen-remodeling approach. Improvement is gradual.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually requires multiple sessions separated by several weeks.
Downtime & Recovery: Redness, swelling or peeling can last several days depending on treatment depth.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Complete removal is unlikely. Laser treatment requires extra care in darker skin because of pigment risk.
FAQs:
Q: Can stretch marks be completely removed?
A: Usually not. Treatment aims to make them less noticeable and improve texture or colour.

Short Description: Non-surgical procedures used to improve the appearance of mild skin laxity on the face or body.
Full Description: Skin tightening is a category that includes radiofrequency, focused ultrasound and some other energy-based technologies. Outcomes depend on the degree of laxity, treatment area, device and patient factors.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Mild facial laxity
2. Neck laxity
3. Mild body skin laxity
4. Early age-related loss of firmness
Key Benefits:
• Non-surgical approach
• Can stimulate collagen remodeling
• Usually less recovery than surgery
What To Expect: The clinician assesses laxity and selects an energy-based device. Treatment generally produces controlled heating or focused energy without an incision.
Sessions & Frequency: Some devices use a single treatment while others require 2–6 sessions; maintenance may be recommended.
Downtime & Recovery: Usually minimal downtime; temporary redness, swelling or tenderness may occur.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Energy settings must be appropriate to avoid burns. Severe laxity may respond better to surgery than non-surgical treatment.
FAQs:
Q: Can skin tightening remove large amounts of loose skin?
A: Non-surgical tightening is generally best for mild to moderate laxity and cannot replicate surgical skin removal.

Short Description: Treatment for focal hyperhidrosis using medical therapies or procedures chosen according to the affected area.
Full Description: Hyperhidrosis is excessive sweating beyond what is needed for temperature regulation. Treatment may include topical antiperspirants, iontophoresis, botulinum toxin injections, oral medicines or selected device-based options.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Underarm sweating
2. Palmar sweating
3. Plantar sweating
4. Other focal hyperhidrosis
Key Benefits:
• Can substantially reduce sweating in treated areas
• Multiple treatment options exist
• Treatment can be tailored to the body site
What To Expect: The clinician identifies the distribution and severity of sweating. For botulinum toxin, small injections are placed in the affected area; iontophoresis uses a low electrical current through water.
Sessions & Frequency: Botulinum toxin commonly lasts several months; iontophoresis requires an initial series followed by maintenance.
Downtime & Recovery: Injection-site pain or bruising can occur with botulinum toxin. Iontophoresis can cause temporary skin irritation.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Underlying medical causes and medicines should be considered. Botulinum toxin must be administered in a medical setting.
FAQs:
Q: Does Botox help excessive sweating?
A: Yes. Botulinum toxin can temporarily block the nerve signals that stimulate sweat glands in treated areas.

Short Description: Personalized treatment for under-eye pigmentation, hollowness, fine lines or texture after identifying the underlying cause.
Full Description: Dark circles and under-eye ageing have multiple causes, including pigment, visible vessels, shadowing from hollowness, thin skin and lifestyle factors. Treatment may involve skincare, lasers, fillers or other procedures depending on the cause.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Under-eye pigmentation
2. Tear-trough hollowness
3. Fine lines
4. Thin or crepey skin
Key Benefits:
• Targets the specific cause rather than treating all dark circles alike
• Can improve the appearance of selected under-eye concerns
• Treatment can be conservative and staged
What To Expect: The clinician examines pigment, vascular visibility, volume and skin texture. Treatment is chosen only after identifying the dominant contributor.
Sessions & Frequency: Varies by treatment; injectable or device-based plans may require one or several sessions.
Downtime & Recovery: Depends on modality; fillers can cause swelling/bruising, while topical/laser treatments have different recovery profiles.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • The under-eye area is anatomically sensitive. Filler carries rare but serious vascular risks and should only be performed by highly experienced injectors.
FAQs:
Q: Will filler fix every type of dark circle?
A: No. Filler mainly addresses volume-related shadowing and does not directly treat every pigment or vascular cause.

Short Description: Diagnosis-led approach for darkened lips using trigger control, topical care and selected procedures.
Full Description: Lip pigmentation can result from genetics, sun exposure, irritation, smoking, inflammation or medications. Treatment should address the cause before considering cosmetic procedures such as carefully selected peels or lasers.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Post-inflammatory lip pigmentation
2. Sun-related darkening
3. Selected cosmetic pigmentation concerns
4. Pigmentation after irritation
Key Benefits:
• Can improve uneven lip colour when the cause is treatable
• Addresses underlying triggers
• Procedures can be selected conservatively
What To Expect: The lips are examined for inflammation, dryness, medication exposure and other causes. If a procedure is appropriate, it is performed conservatively because lip tissue is sensitive.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually requires several treatments if a procedure is used; exact frequency depends on cause and modality.
Downtime & Recovery: Dryness, irritation, swelling or peeling can occur depending on treatment.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Active lip dermatitis, infection or unexplained persistent pigmentation should be assessed before cosmetic treatment. Sun protection for the lips is important.
FAQs:
Q: Can lip pigmentation always be removed?
A: No. Some causes are chronic or genetic, and aggressive treatment can itself cause irritation and more pigmentation.

Short Description: Treatment planning for neck lines, pigmentation, texture and mild laxity.
Full Description: Neck ageing can involve horizontal lines, sun damage, pigmentation, skin laxity and platysmal muscle activity. Different concerns require different treatments, including skincare, injectables or energy-based procedures.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Neck lines
2. Mild neck laxity
3. Uneven pigmentation
4. Photoaging and texture changes
Key Benefits:
• Targets specific signs of neck ageing
• Non-surgical options are available for selected concerns
• Can combine skin-quality and tightening approaches
What To Expect: The clinician examines skin quality, muscle activity and laxity before choosing a treatment. The neck is more sensitive than many facial areas, so conservative treatment is common.
Sessions & Frequency: Depends on the concern and modality; may require a series or periodic maintenance.
Downtime & Recovery: Ranges from none to several days depending on treatment.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Neck anatomy includes important blood vessels and nerves. Treatment should be performed by an experienced clinician with anatomy-specific planning.
FAQs:
Q: Is one treatment enough for neck ageing?
A: Usually not for every concern. Neck lines, laxity and pigmentation may require different or combined approaches.

Short Description: Treatment for age-related changes in the hands including volume loss, pigmentation and skin texture.
Full Description: Hand ageing can involve thinning skin, visible veins/tendons, pigmentation and loss of soft-tissue volume. Management may include photoprotection, pigment treatments, energy devices or fillers in selected cases.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Volume loss on the backs of hands
2. Sun spots
3. Thin or crepey skin
4. Uneven texture
Key Benefits:
• Can restore selected lost volume
• May reduce the appearance of sun-related pigment
• Improves skin quality in selected patients
What To Expect: The hands are assessed for volume, vessels, tendons and pigment. Treatment is selected according to the dominant concern.
Sessions & Frequency: Fillers may be one treatment with review; pigment/skin-quality procedures often require a series.
Downtime & Recovery: Swelling and bruising are possible after injections; laser/peel recovery depends on modality.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Hand filler requires knowledge of complex anatomy and vascular structures. Pigment treatments can cause post-inflammatory colour change.
FAQs:
Q: What does hand rejuvenation actually treat?
A: It can address volume loss, pigmentation and skin quality, but the best approach depends on which changes are most prominent.

Short Description: Personalized treatment to make scars less noticeable by improving texture, colour or contour.
Full Description: Scar revision is a broad term covering procedures such as laser resurfacing, microneedling, subcision, steroid injections or surgical revision. The correct approach depends on whether the scar is raised, depressed, widened, pigmented or red.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Acne scars
2. Depressed traumatic scars
3. Raised scars/keloids
4. Surgical scars
Key Benefits:
• Can improve scar texture, colour or contour
• Treatment is matched to scar type
• Combination therapy is often useful for complex scars
What To Expect: The clinician evaluates scar type, maturity, colour, thickness and skin tone before selecting treatment. Scar remodeling is gradual.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually multiple sessions for non-surgical approaches; surgical revision has a different timeline.
Downtime & Recovery: Varies widely from a few days to several weeks depending on procedure.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • No procedure guarantees complete scar removal. Raised scars may require medical injections or other specialized treatment rather than resurfacing alone.
FAQs:
Q: Can a scar be completely removed?
A: Usually not. The aim is to make the scar less noticeable and improve its texture, colour or contour.

Short Description: Procedural treatment aimed at reducing the appearance of established stretch marks.
Full Description: Established stretch marks are dermal scars. Revision treatments such as microneedling, fractional laser and radiofrequency can stimulate remodeling, but improvement is gradual and complete removal is unlikely.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Established white stretch marks
2. Textural irregularity
3. Broad areas of striae
Key Benefits:
• Can improve texture and visibility
• May reduce contrast between stretch marks and surrounding skin
• Multiple modalities can be considered
What To Expect: Treatment is performed over the affected area using a selected remodeling device. Several sessions are usually needed to see meaningful change.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually a course of multiple treatments spaced several weeks apart.
Downtime & Recovery: Redness, swelling or peeling can occur for several days.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Treatment should be individualized to skin tone and striae type. Laser treatment may have greater pigment risk in darker skin.
FAQs:
Q: Is stretch-mark revision the same as stretch-mark removal?
A: No. Treatments aim to make stretch marks less noticeable rather than erase them completely.

Short Description: Treatment to reduce the appearance of enlarged pores by addressing oil, congestion, texture and collagen support.
Full Description: Pore size is influenced by genetics, sebum production, follicular structure and skin ageing. Treatment can make pores less noticeable but cannot permanently eliminate normal skin pores.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Visible facial pores
2. Oily skin
3. Comedonal congestion
4. Uneven texture
Key Benefits:
• Can reduce visible congestion
• May smooth surrounding texture
• Can improve the appearance of pores through collagen remodeling
What To Expect: The clinician determines whether oil, congestion or loss of skin firmness is the main contributor. Treatment may combine home skincare with procedures.
Sessions & Frequency: Varies by treatment; peels may be repeated every few weeks and collagen-remodeling procedures usually require a series.
Downtime & Recovery: Ranges from none to several days depending on modality.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Avoid aggressive squeezing. Treatment should account for acne, sensitivity and pigment risk.
FAQs:
Q: Can pores be permanently closed?
A: No. Pores are normal skin structures. Treatment can reduce their appearance rather than eliminate them.

Short Description: Treatment category for roughness, uneven surface texture and visible fine lines.
Full Description: Uneven texture can result from acne scars, enlarged pores, photodamage, dryness or ageing. Treatment is chosen according to the cause and may include skincare, peels, microneedling, RF microneedling or laser resurfacing.
Common Uses / Indications:
1. Rough skin surface
2. Acne-scar texture
3. Enlarged pores
4. Fine lines and photoaging
Key Benefits:
• Smooths selected surface irregularities
• Can stimulate collagen remodeling
• Allows treatment to be tailored to the underlying cause
What To Expect: The clinician assesses whether texture is superficial, scar-related or caused by laxity. The selected procedure is then performed at an appropriate intensity.
Sessions & Frequency: Usually a series for collagen-remodeling treatments; superficial exfoliation may be repeated more frequently.
Downtime & Recovery: Depends on modality, from minimal redness to several days of peeling or erythema.
Clinical Considerations & Precautions: • Active acne or inflammatory skin disease may need treatment first. Laser and deeper procedures carry greater pigment risk in darker skin.
FAQs:
Q: What is the best treatment for uneven texture?
A: It depends on the cause. Acne scars, pores, dryness and photoaging can require different treatments.
